passage:
Ankita: before we lock the venue plan, Madhuri, can you argue against it tomorrow? Take the other side, whatever you honestly think.
Madhuri: really? I do have a few doubts about the outdoor stage 😅
Ankita: that's exactly what I want. Everyone else, please listen first. I'll speak last.
Dev: ok
Nisha: I like the outdoor stage but fine
(next day)
Madhuri: Rain risk, sound, and only one exit. That's my case.
Nisha: ...the exit thing is actually a real problem
Dev: hadn't thought about the sound
Ankita: Thank you Madhuri. That changed my mind about two things 🙂

qa.q: What three problems did Madhuri name against the outdoor stage?
qa.a: Madhuri named rain risk, sound, and only one exit.

qa.q: Why does Ankita ask Madhuri to argue against the plan and promise to speak last?
qa.a: Ankita wants honest doubts to come out and does not want Ankita's own view to shape the others first, showing a wish to make dissent safe.

qa.q: What did Ankita do after hearing Madhuri that kept the habit alive?
qa.a: Ankita thanked Madhuri and said the argument changed two of Ankita's views, which shows that raising problems is valued, not punished.

qa.q: What might Madhuri feel when asked to take the other side and then thanked?
qa.a: Madhuri probably feels a little nervous at first and then valued, since doubts about the stage were welcome rather than called negative.

grounding: One person planning an event asks someone to argue against the plan, speaks last and thanks the person who raises problems, making dissent safe.

passage: In the panchayat hall of a small village, the cooperative's secretary Rajni was about to close the meeting on buying a shared tractor. Fifteen farmers nodded, and the sarpanch spoke loudest in favour. Rajni raised a hand. "Pallavi, you keep the accounts and you always find problems. Please argue against the tractor for five minutes. I will speak last." Pallavi smiled and stood. "Who drives it in the sowing week, who pays for repairs, and what if the rains are late?" The hall shifted. A young farmer, Ganesh, murmured, "She is right." When Rajni finally spoke, it was to say, "Thank you, Pallavi. Now we decide with our eyes open."

qa.q: What did Rajni ask Pallavi to do for five minutes?
qa.a: Rajni asked Pallavi to argue against the tractor for five minutes.

qa.q: Why does Rajni speak last and ask Pallavi to argue against the tractor?
qa.a: Rajni seems uneasy that everyone is agreeing so quickly and wants the group's confidence tested without steering the room; the request shows a belief that honest problems protect the cooperative.

qa.q: What did Rajni do at the end that kept dissent normal?
qa.a: Rajni thanked Pallavi and said the decision would now be made with eyes open, treating the problems as help rather than disloyalty.

qa.q: What might Ganesh be feeling when murmuring "She is right"?
qa.a: Ganesh probably feels relieved and a little surprised that the doubts Ganesh may have had were spoken aloud by someone else.

grounding: A cooperative's secretary invites someone to argue against the plan, speaks last and thanks the person who raises problems.

passage:
In a small design studio in Osaka, Layla pinned the new café logo on the wall. Everyone loved it. Kenji clapped. Mariko said, “Perfect.”
Layla held up a hand. “Aiko, would you do me a favour? Argue against it. Pretend you hate it. Give me three reasons.”
Aiko laughed, surprised, then took it seriously. “It's hard to read from across the street. Red looks like a warning. And it's a lot like the bakery next door.”
Nobody spoke for a moment. Then Kenji said, “The bakery thing is true.”
Layla spoke last. “Thank you, Aiko. That's exactly why I asked.” She changed the colour and the font that week. The café owner said, “Now I can see it from the station.”

qa.q: What did Aiko say the red looked like?
qa.a: Aiko said red looks like a warning.

qa.q: How did Aiko seem to feel when Layla asked for an argument against the logo?
qa.a: Aiko seemed surprised at first, then comfortable and trusted enough to take the role seriously.

qa.q: Which of Layla's choices made disagreement feel safe?
qa.a: She asked someone to argue against the plan, spoke last herself, and thanked Aiko openly for raising problems.

qa.q: How might Kenji and Mariko have felt after Aiko's points?
qa.a: They may have felt a little embarrassed at first, then glad the flaws were caught before the café owner saw them.

grounding: Shows a lead who asks someone to argue against a popular plan, speaks last and thanks the critic, making dissent normal.

passage:
The school timetable committee met in the staffroom after last bell. Tejas, the youngest head of department, had drafted a new timetable. Everyone seemed ready to sign.
“Before anyone says yes,” Tejas said, “Parveen ma'am, would you be our devil's advocate today? Find everything wrong with it.”
Parveen raised an eyebrow, then smiled. “Happily. Grade 6 has maths in the last period four days a week. They'll be asleep. And the lab is double-booked on Thursdays.”
Two teachers laughed in surprise. One said, “She's right about Thursdays.”
Tejas waited until everyone had spoken. Then he said, “Thank you, Parveen ma'am. Let's rotate the role every meeting.” The committee fixed both problems before the new term.

qa.q: Which day was the lab double-booked?
qa.a: The lab was double-booked on Thursdays.

qa.q: How did Parveen seem to feel about playing devil's advocate?
qa.a: She seemed amused and pleased, raising an eyebrow and then smiling as she said "Happily".

qa.q: Why was rotating the role a smart next step?
qa.a: It makes dissent a normal part of every meeting, so no single person is seen as the negative one.

qa.q: How might the Grade 6 students be affected by the committee's change?
qa.a: They won't be stuck with tired last-period maths four days a week, so their learning is likely to be better.

grounding: Shows a young department head inviting a devil's advocate, speaking last and thanking the critic so dissent is safe.

passage:
Subject: Tomorrow's planning meeting – a request
Hi team,
Tomorrow we decide the new volunteer schedule for the shelter. I know most of us like the draft, including me, and that's exactly why I'm a bit worried.
Binita, would you be our official critic tomorrow? Please come ready to pick holes in the plan as hard as you can. Everyone else, I'll ask for your concerns first, and I'll speak last, so my opinion doesn't shape yours.
If you raise a problem, you're helping, not being negative. I'll say thank you, and I mean it.
Last year we agreed too quickly and ran short on Sunday nights for two months. Let's not repeat that.
See you at ten,
Elizabeth

qa.q: Which nights were short of volunteers last year?
qa.a: They ran short on Sunday nights for two months.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth worried about before the meeting?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt uneasy that because most people liked the draft, the team might agree too quickly again, as it did last year.

qa.q: What makes Elizabeth's email a good way to prepare a meeting?
qa.a: It asks Binita to argue against the plan, promises to speak last and thanks problem-raisers in advance, so dissent feels safe.

qa.q: How might Binita feel about being asked to be the critic?
qa.a: Binita might feel trusted and a bit nervous, but relieved that the objections will be welcomed rather than seen as negativity.

grounding: A lead writes to the team asking one member to argue against the plan, promising to speak last and thank those who raise problems.

passage:
People ask what changed in my team, and honestly, it was one Tuesday.
I'm Uday. I run a small design team at a logistics company, and back then every idea of mine got a round of "great, let's do it." It felt nice. It also nearly lost us a client.
So now, before we lock a plan, I say, "Vishal, today you're the opposition. Tear this apart." The first time, Vishal laughed, then found three real holes in ten minutes. Meena and Kiran joined in once they saw nobody got in trouble for it.
I keep my own opinion till the very end, because once I speak, people drift toward me. And after the meeting I thank whoever raised the hardest problem, by name, in the team chat.
It's a small habit. But now Kiran brings me bad news early, and that's worth more to me than applause.

qa.q: Whom does Uday ask to argue against the plan?
qa.a: Vishal, who is told "today you're the opposition."

qa.q: How did Uday feel back when every idea got "great, let's do it"?
qa.a: Uday felt pleased and comfortable, which is exactly why the danger went unnoticed until a client nearly left.

qa.q: Why does Uday share an opinion only at the very end of the meeting?
qa.a: Once the lead speaks, people drift toward that view; speaking last lets honest views come out first.

qa.q: What is it like for Kiran to work in Uday's team now?
qa.a: Kiran seems to feel safe bringing bad news early, trusting it will be thanked rather than punished 🙂

grounding: Shows a lead who assigns someone to argue against the plan, speaks last and publicly thanks those who raise problems, making dissent normal.
